A chemical bond can be considered as the “glue” that holds atoms together 
in molecules (covalent or polar covalent bonding), in ionic compounds 
(ionic bonding) and in metals (metallic bonding). Chemical bonding is best 
described as a continuum between all three models. With the exception of 
pure covalent or pure metallic bonding in some elementary substances, most 
chemical bonds have mixed character. For example, polar covalent bonds 
are intermediate between covalent and ionic (table 11) while bonding in 
metalloids is intermediate between metallic and covalent.

* considering the metallic and non-metallic character of participating 
species (table 11) 
* using the difference in electronegativity values (Ay) as an approximate

&) onding models (ionic, covalent and metallic) can be used to explain \ 
the properties of various materials. 
* Why do ionic substances such as sodium chloride, NaCl, have high 
melting points? This is discussed in Structure 2.7, and is related to 
the strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely 
charged ions. 
* Why do covalent substances such as sugar (sucrose), CH-0., 
have low melting points? This is discussed in Structure 2.2, and is 
related to weak intermolecular forces of attraction. 
* Why do some substances with covalent network structure, such 
as diamond, have very high melting points? This is discussed in 
Structure 2.2, and is related to the fact that the strong covalent 
bonds within the network must be broken before melting occurs. 
* Why are metals such as aluminium, Al, malleable? This is discussed 
in Structure 2.3, and is related to the non-directional nature of metallic 
bonding, which allows the cations to slide past one another. \ P

Alloys and their properties 
Alloys are produced by fusing a metal with other metallic or non-metallic 
elements, which alters the structure and properties of the original metal. Alloys 
often have greater mechanical strength than their individual components 
because ions of different sizes form a less regular lattice, in which itis more 
difficult for the layers of cations to slide past one another. For example, 
steel is stronger than iron; stainless steel resists corrosion; brass and bronze 
are stronger, harder and more resistant to corrosion than copper; traces of 
titanium or scandium added to aluminium greatly increase its strength without 
compromising its low density for use in aircraft bodies. 
Polymers 
* Polymers are large molecules (macromolecules) that consist of 
repeating subunits connected to one another by covalent bonds. 
* A macromolecule may or may not contain repeating subunits. 
All polymers are macromolecules but not all macromolecules 
are polymers. 
Polymers are made up of repeating subunits (say A®). The small molecule from 
which the polymer is made is termed the monomer (say A). The repeating 
subunit is derived from the monomer, but the structures of repeating unitand 
monomer are not identical.

Assessment tip 
Do not mix up the term repeating subunit with the term monomer. A monomer 
is a small molecule of the reactant from which the polymer is synthesized. 
A repeating subunit is a part of the polymer macromolecule, in which many 
repeating subunits are linked by covalent bonds and form a long chain or 
network. For example, the monomer of polyethene is ethene, H,C=CH,, but 
the repeating subunit in polyethene is —CH,—CH,—, in which the double 
bond has been broken in order to form single covalent bonds with other 
subunits. The structure of polyethene can be written as —{—CHZ_CHZ_},T' 
where n is the degree of polymerization. When representing a polymer, 
square brackets, continuation bonds and n should always be included.

2.4 From models to materials 
The size and structure of A® units determine the physical and chemical 
properties of the polymer. In addition, the properties of a polymer depend on 
the degree of polymerization (the n value) and cross-linking (covalent bonding) 
between chains. Polymers with greater n values have higher melting points, 
mechanical strength and rigidity because of the stronger London (dispersion) 
forces of attraction between their longer chains. Cross-linking also increases 
the melting points, strength and rigidity of polymers because additional 
covalent bonds between polymer chains are stronger than intermolecular 
forces and therefore require more energy to break. 
In contrast, polymers without cross-links are usually soft, flexible and 
non-elastic, and their melting points are relatively low. Such polymers 
can be reshaped easily, and they are most suitable for recycling. 
Polymers can be classified as natural or synthetic, depending on whether 
or not they occur naturally (table 12); and also as addition or condensation 
polymers (AHL Structure 2.4), depending on how they are made (table 13).

The periodic table represents the periodic law, which states that the chemical 
and physical properties of the elements recur periodically when the elements 
are arranged in increasing order of their atomic numbers, Z. This recurrence 
defines the structure of the periodic table, which consists of horizontal periods, 
vertical groups and rectangular blocks (figure 1).

Ions of aluminium and those of other metals have different sizes, so the lattice of an aluminium alloy is less regular than the lattice of pure aluminium. The layers of cations in the alloy cannot slide past one another as easily as those in aluminium, so a sample of the alloy is less likely to be deformed without cracking.
